questions.why: The else belongs to the nearest if, which is if(b). If a is false, the inner if is never reached, so neither s1 nor s2 runs.

questions.q: Output: `switch(3){case 1: printf("a"); case 3: printf("b"); case 4: printf("c"); break; default: printf("d");}`
questions.why: The value 3 matches case 3, which prints b. With no break it falls into case 4 and prints c, then the break stops it. The output is bc.

questions.q: Number of times `x++` executes: `for(i=1;i<=n;i++) for(j=1;j<=i;j++) x++;` with n = 10
questions.why: The inner loop runs i times for each i, so the total is 1 + 2 + … + 10 = 10 × 11/2 = 55.

questions.q: Iterations of `for(i=1;i<1000;i*=2)`?
questions.why: i takes 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256 and 512, and 1024 fails i < 1000. That's 10 values.

questions.q: Assertion: `while(1);` hangs the program. Reason: the semicolon is an empty body and 1 is always true.
questions.why: The assertion is true: while(1); has an empty body and a condition that is always true, so it loops forever. The reason explains exactly why.

questions.q: Value of s: `int s=0; for(int i=1;i<=10;i++){ if(i%2) continue; s+=i; }`
questions.why: When i is odd (i%2 is non-zero), continue skips it. So only even numbers are added: 2 + 4 + 6 + 8 + 10 = 30.

questions.q: Case: A menu must show at least once and repeat until the user enters 0. Best loop?
questions.why: A menu must be shown before the exit test, and repeated until 0 is entered. A do-while checks the condition after the body, so it fits.

questions.q: Output: `int i; for(i=0;i<3;i++); printf("%d", i);`
questions.why: The semicolon after the for makes an empty loop body, so the printf runs only once, after the loop. The loop ends when i reaches 3, so it prints 3.

questions.q: Value of k after `int k=0; for(int i=0;i<5;i++) for(int j=0;j<5;j++){ if(j==i) break; k++; }`
questions.why: For row i the inner loop does k++ for j = 0..i−1, then breaks when j == i. That gives 0 + 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10.

questions.q: Which condition correctly checks that x lies strictly between 10 and 20?
questions.why: For 'strictly between' both tests must hold, so use &&: x > 10 && x < 20. With || almost every x passes, and 10 < x < 20 doesn't work in C.

questions.q: Number of iterations of `for(i=n; i>0; i/=2)` in terms of n (n ≥ 1)?
questions.why: Halving n until it reaches 0 takes ⌊log₂ n⌋ + 1 steps. For n = 8: 8, 4, 2, 1 gives 4 iterations, and log₂8 + 1 = 4.

questions.q: Output: `int x=1; while(x<100) x = x*3 + 1; printf("%d", x);`
questions.why: x goes 1 → 1·3+1 = 4 → 13 → 40 → 121. Since 121 is not less than 100, the loop stops and prints 121.

questions.q: Total times inner body runs: `for(i=1;i<=n;i*=2) for(j=0;j<n;j++) work();`
questions.why: The outer loop doubles i, so it runs about log n times. The inner loop runs n times for each, so the total is Θ(n log n).

courses.title: Unit 3 · Functions, Scope, Storage Classes and Recursion
courses.summary: Function declaration and definition, call by value, scope and lifetime, the four storage classes, and recursion with tracing of the call stack — a favourite of GATE output-prediction questions.
outcomes: Learners can declare, define and call functions with prototypes
Learners can explain call by value and simulate call by reference with pointers
Learners can distinguish auto, static, extern and register
Learners can write and trace recursive functions and their recurrences

scenes.text: Farhan pastes the same 15-line GST calculation in five places. A rate change means editing all five, and he misses one.
He moves it into one function, calculate_gst(), and now a single change fixes every place.

steps.title: Parts of a function
steps.body:
- **Prototype** (declaration): `int square(int x);` tells the compiler the name, return type and parameter types.
- **Definition**: `int square(int x) { return x * x; }`
- **Call**: `y = square(5);` — 5 is the **argument**, x is the **parameter**.
- `void` return type means no value; `f(void)` means no parameters.
- A function can return only one value directly (use pointers or structs for more).

steps.title: Call by value
steps.body:
C passes **copies** of arguments. Changing a parameter inside the function does not change the caller's variable.

To let a function modify caller data, pass the **address**: `void inc(int *p) { (*p)++; }` called as `inc(&n);` — this is often called call by reference, though technically the pointer itself is passed by value.

steps.title: Solved example: swap that fails and swap that works
steps.body:
```
void swap1(int a, int b){ int t=a; a=b; b=t; }
void swap2(int *a, int *b){ int t=*a; *a=*b; *b=t; }
```
x = 1, y = 2:
- `swap1(x, y)` swaps the copies only → x = 1, y = 2.
- `swap2(&x, &y)` swaps through the addresses → x = 2, y = 1.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling a function before its prototype or definition is visible.
- Forgetting `return` in a non-void function — using the result is undefined.
- Returning the address of a local variable — it dies when the function returns.
- Assuming argument evaluation order: in `f(i++, i++)` the order is unspecified (and here undefined).

steps.title: Good design
steps.body: One function, one job. A function name should read like a verb: `read_marks`, `is_prime`, `print_report`.

activity.prompt: Complete `long long power(int base, int exp)` (exp ≥ 0) using a loop, and print power(a, b) for the input pair. `2 10` → 1024.
activity.hint: Start r at 1, multiply by base exp times.

quiz.q: C passes arguments to functions by…
quiz.why: C always passes arguments by value: the function gets copies. To change the caller's variable, you pass its address (a pointer).

quiz.q: A function prototype tells the compiler…
options: Name, return type and parameter types
quiz.why: A prototype declares the function's name, return type and parameter types, so the compiler can check calls before it sees the body.

quiz.q: After `void f(int a){a=10;}` and `int x=5; f(x);` x is…
quiz.why: f gets a copy of x, so a = 10 changes only the copy. The caller's x stays 5.

quiz.q: Returning the address of a local (auto) variable leads to…
quiz.why: An automatic local variable is destroyed when the function returns. A pointer to it then points to invalid memory, which is a dangling pointer.

quiz.q: Correct call to `void inc(int *p)` for int n?
quiz.why: inc takes an int*, so you pass the address of n with &n. Passing n gives an int, and *n isn't valid for an int.

scenes.text: Lata wants a function that counts how many times it has been called, but her counter resets to 0 every call.
Adding the word static keeps the counter alive between calls, while still hiding it from the rest of the program.

steps.title: Scope vs lifetime
steps.body:
- **Scope** = where a name is visible (block, function, file).
- **Lifetime** = how long the storage exists (automatic: while the block runs; static: whole program run).
- An inner block variable **shadows** an outer one of the same name.

steps.title: The four storage classes
steps.body:
- `auto` — default for locals; garbage value if uninitialised; lives in the block (stack).
- `register` — hint to keep in a CPU register; you cannot take its address with &.
- `static` (local) — initialised once (default 0), keeps value across calls. `static` at file level — **internal linkage**: hidden from other files.
- `extern` — declares a variable defined elsewhere (another file); no storage allocated by the declaration.
- Global variables have static lifetime and default to 0.

steps.title: Solved example: static counter
steps.body:
```
int next(void){ static int c = 0; c++; return c; }
```
- Call 1: c initialised to 0 once, becomes 1 → returns 1.
- Call 2: c keeps 1, becomes 2 → returns 2.
- `printf("%d %d %d", next(), next(), next());` — argument evaluation order is unspecified, so call them in separate statements for predictable output.

steps.title: Solved example: shadowing
Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Expecting uninitialised local variables to be zero.
- Writing `extern int n = 5;` inside a function (initialising an extern there is an error).
- Overusing globals: makes code hard to test and reason about.

activity.prompt: Write `int tick(void)` using a static local so that calling it 4 times in separate statements prints 1 2 3 4 (one per line).
activity.hint: static int c = 0; is initialised only once.

quiz.q: Default initial value of a static local int?
quiz.why: Variables with static storage duration are zero-initialised by default, so a static local int starts at 0. An ordinary auto local would hold garbage.

quiz.q: You cannot apply & to a variable declared…
quiz.why: A register variable may live in a CPU register, so it may have no memory address. C therefore forbids using & on it.

quiz.q: A static global variable is visible…
quiz.why: static on a global gives it internal linkage, so the name is visible only within its own source file.
extern int n; only declares that n exists and is defined in some other place. It doesn't create the variable or allocate storage.

quiz.q: Lifetime of an auto local variable?
quiz.why: An auto local variable is created when its block starts and destroyed when the block ends.

lessons.title: Recursion: base case, call stack and tracing

scenes.text: Meenal opens a nesting doll, finds a smaller one, opens it, and keeps going until the tiniest doll that cannot open.
That smallest doll is the base case. Recursion works the same way: solve a smaller version until it is trivial.

steps.title: What recursion needs
steps.body:
- A **base case** that returns without recursing.
- A **recursive case** that moves toward the base case.
- Each call gets its own **stack frame** (parameters, locals, return address). Too deep → stack overflow.

`int fact(int n){ if (n <= 1) return 1; return n * fact(n - 1); }`

steps.title: Solved example: trace fact(4)
steps.body:
- fact(4) = 4 × fact(3)
- fact(3) = 3 × fact(2)
- fact(2) = 2 × fact(1)
- fact(1) = 1 (base)
- Unwind: 2 × 1 = 2 → 3 × 2 = 6 → 4 × 6 = **24**. Maximum stack depth = 4.

steps.title: Solved example: print order
steps.body:
```
void f(int n){ if(n==0) return; f(n-1); printf("%d ", n); }
```
f(3): calls go down to f(0) first, printing happens while unwinding → **1 2 3**.
If printf comes *before* the call, output is 3 2 1.

Fibonacci `fib(n)=fib(n-1)+fib(n-2)` makes about φⁿ calls (exponential) — fib(5) makes 15 calls.

steps.title: Recurrences of common recursive functions
steps.body:
- fact: T(n) = T(n−1) + c → O(n).
- Binary search: T(n) = T(n/2) + c → O(log n).
- Naive fib: T(n) = T(n−1) + T(n−2) + c → O(φⁿ), φ ≈ 1.618.
- Tower of Hanoi: T(n) = 2T(n−1) + 1 → 2ⁿ − 1 moves.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Missing or unreachable base case → infinite recursion, stack overflow.
- Recursing on the same size (`f(n)` calling `f(n)`).
- Using naive recursion for large Fibonacci values — use a loop or memoisation.

activity.prompt: Write a recursive `int gcd(int a, int b)` using Euclid's rule gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b), gcd(a, 0) = a. Print gcd of the two inputs. `84 36` → 12.

quiz.why: A base case stops the recursion by returning without another call. Without it, the function keeps calling itself until the stack overflows.

quiz.q: Output of f(3) where `f(n){ if(n==0) return; printf("%d",n); f(n-1); }`
quiz.why: f prints n before calling f(n−1). So f(3) prints 3, then 2, then 1, and stops at n == 0 without printing. The output is 321.

quiz.q: Moves needed for Tower of Hanoi with 5 discs?
quiz.why: Tower of Hanoi needs 2ⁿ − 1 moves. For 5 discs that is 32 − 1 = 31.

quiz.q: Recursion stores each call's locals on the…
quiz.why: Each function call gets its own stack frame holding its locals and return address, so recursion uses the call stack.

quiz.q: Time complexity of naive recursive Fibonacci?
quiz.why: Each call to fib makes two more calls, and the number of calls grows like φⁿ, so the naive version is exponential. Memoisation brings it to O(n).

scenes.text: In a mock GATE paper Tanvi sees a recursive function with two calls and a static variable, and must find the output.
She draws a recursion tree, labels each call with its argument, and reads the answer off in minutes.

steps.title: Method: draw the recursion tree
steps.body:
- Write each call as a node with its arguments.
- Children = recursive calls in the order they are made.
- Mark where output happens (pre-order = before calls, post-order = after).
- For return values, compute bottom-up from the leaves.

steps.title: Solved example 2: sum of digits recursively
Solved example 3: recursion with a static variable
steps.body:
```
int h(int n){ static int s = 0; if(n==0) return s; s += n; return h(n-1); }
```
- h(3): s = 3 → h(2): s = 5 → h(1): s = 6 → h(0) returns 6.
- Calling h(3) **again** in the same program returns 12, since s is never reset.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting that static variables persist across *all* calls, including later top-level calls.
- Mixing up the number of calls with the return value.
- Ignoring integer division when n is halved (7/2 = 3).

activity.prompt: Write recursive `int binstr(int n)` that prints n in binary (no leading zeros, n ≥ 1). Input 13 → 1101.
activity.hint: Recurse on n/2 before printing n%2 so bits print most-significant first.

quiz.q: Calls made by `g(4)` where g(n) = g(n−1) + g(n−2), base n ≤ 1?

quiz.why: A recursive digit sum adds the last digit to the sum of the rest: 5 + 0 + 9 = 14.
If the print comes after the recursive call, it runs as the calls return, so output appears in the reverse order of the calls.

quiz.q: A static local inside a recursive function is…
quiz.why: A static local has one single instance with static duration, so every call of the function (and every recursion level) shares it.

quiz.q: Depth of recursion of `f(n){ if(n<=1) return; f(n/2); }` for n = 64?
quiz.why: For n = 64 the calls are f(64), f(32), f(16), f(8), f(4), f(2), f(1), which is 7 calls, ending at the base case n <= 1.

questions.q: C's default parameter passing mechanism is…
questions.why: C copies argument values into the parameters, so it uses call by value. Passing pointers lets a function modify the caller's data indirectly.

questions.q: A recursive function must have…
questions.why: A recursive function needs a base case to stop. Without it, it would call itself forever.

questions.q: Default value of a global int?
questions.why: Global variables have static storage and are zero-initialised, so a global int starts at 0.

questions.q: Which storage class gives a file-scope variable internal linkage?
questions.why: Writing static in front of a file-scope variable gives it internal linkage, so other files can't see it.

questions.q: Value of fact(5) using the standard recursive factorial?
Output of `void f(int n){ if(n>0){ f(n-1); printf("%d", n); } }` for f(4)
questions.why: The recursive call is made before printf, so numbers print as the calls return: deepest first. For f(4) the output is 1234.

questions.q: Number of moves for Tower of Hanoi with n discs?
questions.why: To move n discs: move n−1, move the largest, then move n−1 again. So T(n) = 2T(n−1) + 1, which solves to 2ⁿ − 1.

questions.q: Assertion: swap(int a, int b) cannot swap the caller's variables. Reason: C passes copies of arguments.
questions.why: The assertion is true: swap(int a, int b) can't swap the caller's variables. The reason is true and explains it, because a and b are copies, and only the copies get swapped.

questions.q: What does gcd(48, 18) return via Euclid's recursion?
questions.why: Euclid's method: gcd(48,18) → gcd(18,12) → gcd(12,6) → gcd(6,0) = 6.

questions.q: `int f(int n){ static int c=0; c++; if(n<=1) return c; return f(n-1); }` First call f(4) returns…
questions.why: The static variable c is shared across all recursive calls. f(4), f(3), f(2) and f(1) each increment it once, so when n reaches 1 it returns c = 4.

questions.q: With the same f, a second call f(4) in the same program returns…
questions.why: The static c keeps its value between calls. It was 4 after the first call, and the second f(4) adds 4 more increments, so it returns 8.

questions.q: Recurrence for binary search is…
questions.why: Binary search discards half the range after one comparison, so T(n) = T(n/2) + 1, which solves to O(log n).

questions.q: Total calls made by naive fib(6) with base fib(0) = fib(1) returning directly?
questions.why: Count calls with C(n) = 1 + C(n−1) + C(n−2), with C(0) = C(1) = 1: 1, 1, 3, 5, 9, 15, 25. So fib(6) makes 25 calls.

questions.q: Case: A recursive function to sum an array of 10⁷ elements one element per call crashes. Most likely reason?
questions.why: Each recursive call uses a stack frame. Ten million nested calls exceed the typical stack size, causing a stack overflow. A loop avoids it.

questions.q: Return value of `int r(int n){ if(n<10) return n; return r(n/10) + n%10; }` for n = 2026?
questions.why: The function adds the last digit to the sum of the rest: 6 + 2 + 0 + 2 = 10.

questions.q: `int t(int n){ if(n<=0) return 1; return t(n-1) + t(n-2); }` t(3) equals…
Which is true about `register int r;`?
options: r is guaranteed to be in a register
questions.why: A register variable may not have a memory address, so C doesn't allow &r. The compiler isn't forced to use a register either; it's only a hint.

questions.q: Output: `int x=10; void p(void){ printf("%d",x); } int main(void){ int x=20; p(); }`
questions.why: C uses lexical (static) scope. Function p was written where the global x = 10 is visible, so it prints 10, not main's local x.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Arrays and Strings
courses.summary: One- and two-dimensional arrays, row-major address calculation, passing arrays to functions, linear search, bubble sort, and C strings with the standard string functions.
outcomes: Learners can declare, initialise and traverse 1-D and 2-D arrays
Learners can compute element addresses in row-major and column-major order
Learners can pass arrays to functions and explain decay to pointers
Learners can manipulate null-terminated strings safely

scenes.text: Gaurav needs to store marks for 50 students. Declaring m1 to m50 would be absurd.
One array, int marks[50], lets him loop over every student with a single index.

steps.title: Declaring and indexing
steps.body:
- `int a[5];` — 5 contiguous ints; indices 0 to 4.
- `int a[5] = {1, 2};` — remaining elements become 0.
- `int a[] = {3, 1, 4};` — size inferred as 3.
- Number of elements: `sizeof(a) / sizeof(a[0])` (works only where a is a real array, not a pointer parameter).
- C does **no bounds checking**: `a[5]` is undefined behaviour.

steps.title: Address of an element
steps.body:
If the array starts at base address B and each element is w bytes:

**address(a[i]) = B + i × w**

Example: int a[10] at 1000 with 4-byte int: a[6] is at 1000 + 6 × 4 = 1024.

steps.title: Solved example: maximum and its index
steps.body:
a = {4, 9, 2, 9, 7}
- max = a[0] = 4, pos = 0
- i = 1: 9 > 4 → max = 9, pos = 1
- i = 2: 2 no; i = 3: 9 > 9? no (first occurrence kept); i = 4: 7 no
- Result: max 9 at index **1**.

steps.title: Solved example: reverse in place
steps.body:
Swap a[i] with a[n−1−i] for i from 0 to n/2 − 1.
- {1,2,3,4,5}: swap(0,4) → {5,2,3,4,1}; swap(1,3) → {5,4,3,2,1}; middle stays. Done in n/2 swaps.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Looping `i <= n` and reading a[n].
- Using sizeof(arr)/sizeof(arr[0]) inside a function where arr is a parameter (gives pointer size / element size).
- Assigning arrays: `b = a;` is not allowed; copy element by element or use memcpy.

activity.prompt: Read n then n integers. Print the sum, the maximum, and the array reversed (space-separated) on three lines.
activity.hint: Initialise max with a[0], not 0, so negative inputs work.

quiz.why: C arrays are indexed from 0, so an array of 8 elements has valid indices 0 to 7.
When an initialiser lists fewer values than the array size, the remaining elements are set to 0. So a[3] is 0.

quiz.q: Address of a[7] for int (4 bytes) array at 2000?
quiz.why: The address of a[7] is base + 7 × size of element = 2000 + 7 × 4 = 2028.

quiz.q: Does C check array bounds at run time?
quiz.why: C does no automatic bounds checking. Going outside an array is undefined behaviour, which may crash or silently corrupt data.
The array uses 12 × 8 = 96 bytes and one element is 8 bytes, so 96/8 = 12 elements. This trick works only where the array is declared.

scenes.text: A booking app stores seats in rows and columns. Bhavna must find where seat (row 3, column 5) lives in memory.
Knowing that C stores rows one after another, she computes the address with one formula.

steps.title: 2-D arrays in C
steps.body:
- `int m[3][4];` — 3 rows, 4 columns, 12 ints.
- Initialise: `int m[2][3] = {{1,2,3},{4,5,6}};`
- In a declaration with an initialiser, only the first dimension may be omitted: `int m[][3] = {...};`
- C stores 2-D arrays in **row-major** order: all of row 0, then row 1, …

steps.title: Address formulas
steps.body:
Array A[R][C], base B, element size w, 0-based indices:

- **Row-major**: addr(A[i][j]) = B + (i × C + j) × w
- **Column-major** (Fortran, MATLAB): addr(A[i][j]) = B + (j × R + i) × w

If indices start at lower bounds L1, L2: use (i − L1) and (j − L2).

steps.title: Solved example: matrix multiplication
steps.body:
C = A (p×q) × B (q×r): `c[i][j] = Σk a[i][k] × b[k][j]`.
- Possible only when columns of A = rows of B.
- Three nested loops → p × q × r multiplications; for n×n, O(n³).
- [[1,2],[3,4]] × [[5,6],[7,8]] = [[19,22],[43,50]].

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Passing a 2-D array to a function without the column size: the parameter must be `int m[][4]` or `int (*m)[4]`.
- Writing `m[i, j]` — the comma operator makes this `m[j]`.
- Mixing up R and C in the address formula.

activity.prompt: Read a 2×2 matrix A and a 2×2 matrix B (row by row) and print A×B as two lines.
activity.hint: c[i][j] += a[i][k] * b[k][j] over k.

quiz.why: C stores multi-dimensional arrays in row-major order: all the elements of row 0, then row 1, and so on.

quiz.q: Row-major address of A[2][3] in int A[5][6], base 0, w = 4?
quiz.why: Address = base + (row × columns + col) × size = 0 + (2 × 6 + 3) × 4 = 15 × 4 = 60.
For multi-dimensional arrays, only the first dimension may be left out, because the compiler needs the other sizes for address calculation. So int m[][2] is valid.

quiz.q: Multiplications to multiply two n×n matrices by the standard method?
quiz.why: The result has n² entries, and each is a sum of n products, so standard multiplication needs n³ multiplications.
In C, m[1, 2] uses the comma operator, so 1 is discarded and the value is 2. It's the same as m[2], not m[1][2].

lessons.title: Passing arrays, linear search and bubble sort

scenes.text: A teacher's app must find whether roll number 42 is present and also print the list in sorted order.
Arjun writes a search function and a bubble sort, passing the array and its length to each.

steps.title: Arrays decay to pointers
steps.body:
When you pass an array to a function, it **decays** to a pointer to its first element. So:

- `void f(int a[], int n)` is the same as `void f(int *a, int n)`.
- The function can modify the caller's elements.
- The size is lost — always pass n separately.

steps.title: Solved example: linear search
steps.body:
Find 7 in {4, 1, 7, 3}:
- i = 0: 4 ≠ 7; i = 1: 1 ≠ 7; i = 2: 7 = 7 → return 2.
- Best case 1 comparison, worst case n, average about n/2 for a successful search → **O(n)**.

steps.title: Solved example: bubble sort passes
steps.body:
Sort {5, 1, 4, 2} ascending:
- Pass 1: (5,1) swap → 1 5 4 2; (5,4) swap → 1 4 5 2; (5,2) swap → 1 4 2 5. Largest bubbled to the end.
- Pass 2: (1,4) ok; (4,2) swap → 1 2 4 5.
- Pass 3: no swaps → stop early (with a 'swapped' flag).
- Worst case n(n−1)/2 comparisons → O(n²); best case with flag O(n). Stable.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Inner loop bound `j < n` instead of `j < n − 1 − i` → reads past the end.
- Forgetting that the function changes the original array.
- Returning 0 for 'not found' when 0 is a valid index — return −1 instead.

activity.prompt: Implement `void bubble(int a[], int n)` with an early-exit flag. Read n and n numbers, sort, print space-separated.
activity.hint: After pass i, the last i elements are already in place.

quiz.q: When an array is passed to a function, the function receives…
options: A pointer to the first element
quiz.why: An array passed to a function decays to a pointer to its first element. The function doesn't get a copy of the whole array.

quiz.q: Worst-case comparisons of bubble sort on n = 6?
quiz.why: In the worst case bubble sort compares every pair: n(n−1)/2 = 6 × 5/2 = 15.

quiz.q: Best-case complexity of bubble sort with an early-exit flag?
quiz.why: With an early-exit flag, on an already-sorted array the first pass makes no swaps and the sort stops. That is one O(n) pass.

quiz.q: Linear search on unsorted data is…
quiz.why: Linear search may have to look at every element, so it takes O(n) time on unsorted data.
Bubble sort swaps only adjacent elements that are strictly out of order, so equal elements never pass each other. It is stable.

scenes.text: Isha builds a name tag printer. One tag prints her name followed by random symbols.
She forgot space for the terminating '\0'. C strings end where the null character is, nowhere else.

steps.title: What a C string is
steps.body:
- A string is a **char array ending in '\0'** (value 0).
- `char s[] = "cat";` → 4 bytes: 'c','a','t','\0'.
- `char *p = "cat";` → pointer to a string literal; modifying it is undefined behaviour.
- Read a line safely: `fgets(s, sizeof s, stdin);` (keeps the newline). `scanf("%s", s)` stops at whitespace.

steps.title: Key functions
steps.body:
- `strlen(s)` — characters before '\0'.
- `strcpy(d, s)`, `strncpy(d, s, n)` — copy (destination must be large enough).
- `strcat(d, s)` — append.
- `strcmp(a, b)` — 0 if equal, negative if a < b, positive if a > b (lexicographic).
- `strchr(s, c)`, `strstr(s, t)` — search.
- Never compare strings with `==` (it compares addresses).

steps.title: Solved example: own strlen and palindrome
steps.body:
`int len(const char *s){ int n = 0; while (s[n] != '\0') n++; return n; }`

Palindrome check for "level":
- i = 0, j = 4: 'l' = 'l'; i = 1, j = 3: 'e' = 'e'; i = 2 = j → stop → **palindrome**.

strcmp("apple", "apricot"): first difference at index 2, 'p' (112) vs 'r' (114) → negative.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- `char s[5] = "hello";` — no room for '\0' (in C this compiles but the array is not a string).
- `if (s == "yes")` — compares pointers, not contents.
- strcpy into a too-small buffer → buffer overflow, a classic security bug.
- sizeof(s) vs strlen(s): for `char s[20] = "hi"`, sizeof is 20 but strlen is 2.

activity.prompt: Read one word (no spaces) and print `Palindrome` or `Not palindrome`, followed on the next line by its length — without using strlen.
activity.hint: Count characters until '\0', then compare s[i] with s[n-1-i].

quiz.why: A string literal 'India' has 5 letters plus the terminating '\0', so the array needs 6 bytes.
strcmp returns 0 if the two strings have the same contents. A negative or positive value says which one comes first.

quiz.q: `if (a == b)` for two char arrays compares…
quiz.why: Array names decay to addresses, so a == b compares the addresses of two arrays, not their contents. Use strcmp to compare contents.

quiz.q: For `char s[30] = "code";` sizeof(s) and strlen(s) are…
quiz.why: sizeof(s) is the size of the whole array, 30 bytes. strlen counts characters up to the '\0', so 'code' gives 4.

quiz.q: Safer function to read a line with spaces?
quiz.why: fgets reads a line including spaces and takes a buffer size, so it can't overflow. gets has no size limit and was removed in C11, and scanf("%s") stops at spaces.

questions.q: First index of a C array is…
questions.why: The first element of a C array has index 0.

questions.q: String terminator in C is…
questions.why: A C string ends with the null character '\0'. It marks where the string stops.

questions.q: `int a[6] = {1, 2, 3};` sum of all elements?
questions.why: The three listed values are 1, 2, 3 and the remaining three elements are 0. The sum is 1 + 2 + 3 + 0 + 0 + 0 = 6.

questions.q: strlen("hello\0world") is…
questions.why: strlen counts characters up to the first '\0'. In 'hello\0world' that is after 5 characters, so it returns 5.

questions.q: Row-major address of A[4][2] in int A[6][8], base 500, w = 4?
Column-major address of A[4][2] in the same array (R = 6)?
questions.why: In column-major order, address = base + (col × rows + row) × size = 500 + (2 × 6 + 4) × 4 = 500 + 64 = 564.

questions.q: Bubble sort worst-case swaps on n = 5 reverse-sorted elements?
questions.why: In a reverse-sorted array every pair is out of order, so bubble sort needs one swap per pair: 5 × 4/2 = 10.

questions.q: Inside `void f(int a[])`, `sizeof(a)` on a 64-bit system gives…
questions.why: In a function parameter, int a[] is really int *a, so sizeof(a) gives the pointer size, 8 bytes on a 64-bit system, not the array size.

questions.q: Result of strcmp("Zebra", "apple") in ASCII?
questions.why: strcmp compares character codes. 'Z' is 90 and 'a' is 97, so 'Zebra' is less than 'apple', and the result is negative.

questions.q: Assertion: `char *p = "hi"; p[0] = 'H';` is safe. Reason: p points to a char array.
questions.why: The assertion is false: p points to a string literal, which may be stored in read-only memory, so changing p[0] is undefined behaviour. The reason is only partly true: p does point to the characters, but those aren't a modifiable array.

questions.q: Case: A login check uses `if (pwd == "secret")` and always fails. Fix?
questions.why: pwd == "secret" compares two addresses, so it's almost always false. Compare the contents with strcmp(pwd, "secret") == 0.

questions.q: Linear search average comparisons for a successful search, key equally likely anywhere in n items?
questions.why: If the key is equally likely in any position, the average position is (1 + 2 + … + n)/n = (n + 1)/2 comparisons.

questions.q: Output: `char s[] = "abc"; printf("%d", (int)sizeof(s));`
questions.why: The array holds a, b, c and the terminating '\0', so sizeof(s) is 4.

questions.q: For int A[3][4], what is `sizeof(A[0])` with 4-byte int?
questions.why: A[0] is one row of 4 ints, so its size is 4 × 4 = 16 bytes.

questions.q: Lower-bounded array A[1..10][1..15], row-major, base 100, w = 2. Address of A[5][7]?
Multiplying a 3×4 matrix by a 4×2 matrix needs how many scalar multiplications?
questions.why: Multiplying p×q by q×r needs p × q × r scalar multiplications: 3 × 4 × 2 = 24.

questions.q: Which is the declaration of a function taking a 2-D int array with 5 columns?
questions.why: For a 2-D array parameter, the column count must be given so the compiler can compute addresses: int m[][5]. int ** is a different type.

questions.q: Output: `char s[10] = "cat"; strcat(s, "fish"); printf("%zu", strlen(s));`
questions.why: After strcat the string is 'catfish', which has 7 characters. That fits in 10 bytes with the '\0', and strlen gives 7.

courses.title: Unit 5 · Pointers and Dynamic Memory
courses.summary: Pointer basics, pointer arithmetic, the pointer–array relationship, pointers to pointers and function pointers, and dynamic allocation with malloc, calloc, realloc and free — including memory leaks and dangling pointers.
outcomes: Learners can declare and dereference pointers and explain NULL
Learners can apply pointer arithmetic and the identity a[i] == *(a + i)
Learners can read complex declarations such as int (*p)[5] and int *(*f)(int)
Learners can allocate and free heap memory without leaks

scenes.text: Kabir's friend asks for his house. Kabir cannot hand over the house, so he writes down its address.
A pointer is exactly that: a variable holding the address of another variable, so you can reach and change it.

steps.title: Declaring and using pointers
steps.body:
- `int x = 10; int *p = &x;` — p stores the address of x.
- `*p` **dereferences**: it is x itself. `*p = 20;` changes x to 20.
- `&` gives an address; `*` in a declaration means 'pointer to'; in an expression it means 'value at'.
- Print an address with `%p` and cast: `printf("%p", (void*)p);`
- All object pointers on a given platform are typically the same size (e.g., 8 bytes on 64-bit).

steps.title: NULL, wild and dangling pointers
steps.body:
- `int *p = NULL;` — points nowhere; dereferencing NULL is undefined (usually a crash).
- **Wild** pointer: declared but not initialised.
- **Dangling** pointer: points to memory that has been freed or gone out of scope.
- `void *` is a generic pointer: convert to the right type before dereferencing.

steps.title: Solved example: trace
steps.body:
```
int a = 5, b = 7; int *p = &a, *q = &b;
*p = *p + *q;   // a = 12
p = q;          // p now points to b
*p = 1;         // b = 1
```
Final: a = **12**, b = **1**. Note `int *p, q;` declares p as pointer but q as plain int!

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- `int *p; *p = 5;` — writing through a wild pointer.
- `int* p, q;` thinking both are pointers.
- Confusing `*p++` (value at p, then p moves) with `(*p)++` (increments the value).
- Dereferencing a pointer after the variable it points to has gone out of scope.

steps.title: Read declarations right to left
steps.body: `const int *p` — p is a pointer to a const int (value cannot change via p). `int *const p` — p is a const pointer to int (p cannot be re-pointed).

activity.prompt: Write `void minmax(int a[], int n, int *mn, int *mx)` that returns both minimum and maximum through pointers. Read n numbers and print `min max`.
activity.hint: Assign through the pointers with *mn = ...

quiz.why: If p holds the address of x, then *p (dereferencing p) is the object it points to, which is x itself.
In int *p, q; the * belongs only to p. So p is a pointer to int but q is a plain int.

quiz.q: A pointer to freed memory is called…
quiz.why: A pointer that still holds the address of memory that has been freed is a dangling pointer. Using it is undefined behaviour.

options: The int cannot be changed through p
quiz.why: const int *p means p points to a const int, so the int cannot be changed through p. p itself can still be pointed elsewhere.
(*p)++ increments the int that p points to, which is a. So a goes from 3 to 4.

scenes.text: On a street of identical houses, moving 'one house ahead' always means the same number of metres.
p + 1 on an int pointer moves one whole int ahead — four bytes on most machines — not one byte.

steps.title: Arithmetic rules
steps.body:
- `p + k` advances by k **elements**: address + k × sizeof(*p).
- `q − p` (same array) gives the number of elements between them (type ptrdiff_t).
- Allowed: pointer ± integer, pointer − pointer, comparisons within the same array.
- Not allowed: pointer + pointer, multiplying pointers.

steps.title: a[i] is *(a + i)
steps.body:
- The array name in an expression becomes `&a[0]`.
- `a[i]` ≡ `*(a + i)` ≡ `*(i + a)` ≡ `i[a]` (yes, legal!).
- But an array is not a pointer variable: `a = a + 1;` is illegal, and `sizeof a` gives the whole array size.
- `&a` has type 'pointer to array'; `&a + 1` jumps past the **entire** array.

steps.title: Solved example: GATE-style
steps.body:
`int a[] = {10, 20, 30, 40}; int *p = a;` (4-byte int, a at 1000)
- `*(p + 2)` = 30.
- `*p++` → returns 10, then p points to a[1].
- `++*p` → a[1] becomes 21, returns 21.
- `p + 2` holds address 1004 + 8 = 1012.
- `(&a + 1)` is 1000 + 16 = 1016; `*(&a + 1) − 1` points at a[3].

steps.title: Solved example: sum with pointers
steps.body:
```
int sum(int *s, int *e){ int t = 0; while (s < e) t += *s++; return t; }
```
sum(a, a + 4) for {10, 20, 30, 40} → 100. `e` points one past the last element — legal to form, illegal to dereference.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking `p + 1` adds one byte.
- Subtracting pointers from different arrays — undefined.
- `*p++` vs `(*p)++` vs `++*p` — learn precedence: postfix ++ binds tighter than unary *.

activity.prompt: Reverse an array in place using two pointers (no indexing with [] inside the reverse function). Read n and n numbers, print reversed.
activity.hint: Loop while l < r.

quiz.q: If int *p holds 2000 (4-byte int), p + 3 holds…
quiz.why: Pointer arithmetic scales by the size of the type, so p + 3 moves 3 × 4 = 12 bytes: 2000 + 12 = 2012.
By definition a[3] is *(a + 3): the element 3 places after the start of the array.
Adding two pointers has no meaning, so p + q is illegal. You can subtract pointers, compare them, or add an integer to one.
*p++ reads the value at p (5) and then moves p on. So 5 is printed, and p now points to 6.
a[2] means *(a + 2), and addition is commutative, so 2[a] means *(2 + a), which is the same. It is legal, though unusual.

lessons.title: Pointers to pointers, arrays of pointers and function pointers

scenes.text: Riya's calculator should let new operations be added without rewriting the main loop.
She stores pointers to functions in an array and calls ops[choice](a, b). Each new operation is one more entry.

steps.title: Multiple indirection
steps.body:
- `int x = 5; int *p = &x; int **pp = &p;` → `**pp` is x.
- Used when a function must change a caller's pointer (e.g., inserting at the head of a linked list: `void push(Node **head, int v)`).
- `char *names[3] = {"Ann", "Bo", "Cy"};` — array of 3 pointers (jagged strings).
- `int (*q)[4];` — ONE pointer to an array of 4 ints (used for 2-D arrays).

steps.title: Function pointers
steps.body:
- Declaration: `int (*op)(int, int);` — op points to a function taking two ints, returning int.
- Assign: `op = add;` Call: `op(2, 3)` or `(*op)(2, 3)`.
- Real use: `qsort(arr, n, sizeof(int), cmp);` where `int cmp(const void *a, const void *b)` returns negative/zero/positive.

steps.title: Solved example: read declarations (clockwise/spiral)
steps.body:
- `int *a[5]` → a is an array of 5 pointers to int.
- `int (*a)[5]` → a is a pointer to an array of 5 ints.
- `int *f(int)` → f is a function returning pointer to int.
- `int (*f)(int)` → f is a pointer to a function returning int.
- `int (*f[3])(void)` → f is an array of 3 pointers to functions returning int.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing `int *f(int)` when you meant a function pointer — the parentheses around *f matter.
- In qsort comparators, returning `a - b` can overflow for large values; prefer `(a > b) - (a < b)`.
- Forgetting to pass `&head` when the function must update the head pointer.

activity.prompt: Use an array of function pointers `int (*ops[4])(int,int)` for add, sub, mul, max. Read a choice 0–3 and two integers, print the result.
activity.hint: int (*ops[4])(int, int) = { add, sub, mul, mx };

options: Pointer to an array of 10 ints
quiz.why: In int (*p)[10], the parentheses make * bind to p first, so p is a pointer to an array of 10 ints.
In int *p[10], [] binds tighter than *, so p is an array of 10 pointers to int.
pp points to p, and p points to x. *pp is p, and **pp is x.

options: So the function can change the caller's head pointer
quiz.why: C passes by value, so push(Node *head) would change only a copy of the head pointer. Passing Node **head lets push change the caller's head.

quiz.q: The comparator passed to qsort must return…
quiz.why: The comparator for qsort returns a negative, zero or positive int to say less than, equal or greater, as strcmp does.

lessons.title: Dynamic memory: malloc, calloc, realloc, free

scenes.text: Zoya's event app does not know how many guests will register — 10 or 10,000.
She allocates memory on the heap at run time, grows it with realloc when full, and frees it at the end.

steps.title: The four functions (<stdlib.h>)
steps.body:
- `malloc(bytes)` — uninitialised block; returns `void*` or NULL on failure.
- `calloc(n, size)` — n × size bytes, **zero-filled**.
- `realloc(p, newbytes)` — resizes; may move the block; returns NULL on failure (old block remains valid).
- `free(p)` — releases; `free(NULL)` is a safe no-op.
- Memory layout: code, data/BSS (globals, statics), heap (grows), stack (locals, frames).

steps.title: Solved example: dynamic array
Solved example: 2-D array on the heap
steps.body:
R rows × C cols:
- `int **m = malloc(R * sizeof *m);`
- `for (i = 0; i < R; i++) m[i] = malloc(C * sizeof **m);`
- Free in reverse: each row first, then m.
- Alternative single block: `int (*m)[C] = malloc(R * sizeof *m);` — one free, contiguous memory.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- **Memory leak**: losing the last pointer to a block without freeing it.
- **Double free**: calling free twice on the same pointer.
- **Use after free**: dereferencing a dangling pointer.
- `malloc(n)` instead of `malloc(n * sizeof(int))`.
- Freeing memory that was not obtained from malloc/calloc/realloc (e.g., a local array).

steps.title: Why it matters
steps.body: Use-after-free and buffer overflows are among the most common causes of security vulnerabilities in C software. Tools such as Valgrind and AddressSanitizer (`-fsanitize=address`) catch them during testing.

activity.prompt: Read n, allocate an int array of size n with malloc, read n values, print their average with two decimals, then free the memory.
activity.hint: malloc(n * sizeof *a), check for NULL, and cast the sum to double before dividing.

quiz.why: calloc allocates memory and sets all its bytes to zero, but malloc leaves the content uninitialised.
malloc returns NULL if it can't allocate, so you should always check the result before using it.

quiz.q: Losing the only pointer to an allocated block causes…
quiz.why: If you lose the only pointer to an allocated block, it can never be freed, so the memory stays unusable. That's a memory leak.

quiz.q: Why use a temporary with realloc?
options: If realloc fails, the original pointer is not lost
quiz.why: If you write p = realloc(p, n) and realloc fails, it returns NULL and you lose the original pointer, leaking the old block. Use a temporary and check it first.

quiz.q: Where do local variables usually live?
quiz.why: Automatic (local) variables live on the stack, in the frame of the function that declared them.

questions.q: The & operator gives…
questions.why: The & operator gives the address of its operand. The * operator gives the value at an address.

questions.q: Dereferencing a NULL pointer results in…
questions.why: Dereferencing a NULL pointer is undefined behaviour. In practice it usually crashes, but the language doesn't promise any result.

questions.q: If double *d = 1000 (8-byte double), d + 2 is…
questions.why: Adding 2 to a double* moves it by 2 × 8 = 16 bytes: 1000 + 16 = 1016.

questions.q: `int a[]={1,2,3,4}; int *p=a+1; printf("%d", p[1]);` prints…
questions.why: p = a + 1 points to a[1], so p[1] is *(p + 1) = a[2] = 3.

questions.q: Which allocates memory for 10 ints, zero-filled?
questions.why: calloc(10, sizeof(int)) allocates space for 10 ints and sets it all to zero. malloc(10) allocates only 10 bytes and doesn't clear them.

questions.q: `int (*f)(int)` declares f as…
options: Pointer to function taking int, returning int
questions.why: In int (*f)(int), the parentheses make f a pointer, to a function that takes an int and returns an int.

questions.q: Output: `int x=10, *p=&x, **q=&p; **q = 20; printf("%d", x);`
questions.why: q points to p, p points to x, so **q is x. Assigning 20 to it changes x to 20.
&a is a pointer to the whole array, so &a + 1 points just past the array. Cast to int* and subtract 1, you get a[4], which is 5.

questions.q: Assertion: `free(p); free(p);` is harmless. Reason: free checks whether memory was already freed.
questions.why: Both parts are false. Freeing the same pointer twice is undefined behaviour, and free doesn't keep track of what was already freed.

questions.q: Case: a function `int* make(void){ int v = 5; return &v; }` sometimes prints garbage. Cause?
questions.why: v is a local variable and it no longer exists after the function returns, so the returned pointer dangles. Use malloc or a static variable instead.

questions.q: `int a[]={10,20,30}; int *p=a; int y = ++*p;` y and a[0] are…
questions.why: ++*p increments the int that p points to, so a[0] becomes 11, and the expression's value is 11, so y = 11 and a[0] = 11.

questions.q: `int a[]={10,20,30}; int *p=a; int y = *++p;` y is…
questions.why: *++p first moves p to a[1], then dereferences it. So y = 20.

questions.q: With `char *s = "GATE";` what does `printf("%s", s + 2);` print?
questions.why: s + 2 points to the character at index 2, which is 'T', so printf prints the rest of the string, 'TE'.

questions.q: Difference q − p where p = &a[2], q = &a[7] (int a[10])?
questions.why: Pointer subtraction gives the number of elements between them, not bytes: &a[7] − &a[2] = 5.

questions.q: Which declaration is 'array of 3 pointers to functions returning int'?
questions.why: In int (*f[3])(void), f[3] is an array of 3 elements, and each element is a pointer to a function taking no arguments and returning int.

questions.q: On a 64-bit machine, `sizeof(int *)` and `sizeof(char *)` are typically…
questions.why: Pointer size depends on the machine's address width, not on the type it points to. On a 64-bit system, both are 8 bytes.

questions.q: `int *p = malloc(4 * sizeof(int)); p = malloc(8 * sizeof(int));` What problem occurs?
options: Memory leak of the first block
questions.why: The second malloc overwrites p, so the address of the first block is lost and it can never be freed. That's a memory leak.

questions.q: Given `int m[3][4]` and `int (*p)[4] = m;`, `*(*(p + 2) + 1)` refers to…
questions.why: p points to rows of 4 ints. p + 2 is row 2, *(p + 2) is that row, and adding 1 then dereferencing gives column 1, so the element is m[2][1].

courses.title: Unit 6 · Structures, Unions, Enums, Preprocessor and File Handling Concepts
courses.summary: User-defined types (struct, union, enum, typedef), structure padding and sizeof, self-referential structures, the preprocessor and macros, bit manipulation, and the standard file-handling API (fopen/fprintf/fscanf/fclose) explained conceptually.
outcomes: Learners can define and use structures, arrays of structures and pointers to structures
Learners can compute sizeof for structs with padding and for unions
Learners can write safe macros and use conditional compilation
Learners can describe file modes and the file-handling workflow

scenes.text: Harsh keeps name, roll number and CGPA in three separate arrays. Sorting by CGPA scrambles them.
Bundling them into one struct Student keeps each record together, so sorting moves whole records.

steps.title: Defining and using a struct
steps.body:
```
struct Student { int roll; char name[20]; float cgpa; };
struct Student s = {1, "Asha", 8.7f};
typedef struct Student Student;   // now 'Student s2;' works
```
- Member access: `s.roll`; through a pointer: `p->roll` ≡ `(*p).roll`.
- Structs can be assigned (`s2 = s;` copies all members) and passed/returned by value.
- Structs cannot be compared with `==`; compare member by member.

steps.title: Nested and self-referential structs
steps.body:
- Nested: `struct Date { int d, m, y; }; struct Emp { char name[20]; struct Date doj; };` → `e.doj.y`.
- Self-referential: `struct Node { int data; struct Node *next; };` — a struct may contain a **pointer** to its own type (not an instance of itself). This is the basis of linked lists and trees.

steps.title: Solved example: topper from an array of structs
steps.body:
Student s[3] = {{1,"Asha",8.7},{2,"Ben",9.1},{3,"Chi",8.9}};
- best = 0.
- i = 1: 9.1 > 8.7 → best = 1.
- i = 2: 8.9 > 9.1? No.
- Topper: **Ben (roll 2)**. Print with `s[best].name`.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Missing semicolon after the closing brace of a struct definition.
- `p.roll` when p is a pointer (use `p->roll`).
- Assigning strings: `s.name = "Ravi";` is illegal; use `strcpy(s.name, "Ravi");`.
- Passing large structs by value repeatedly — pass a pointer (const if read-only).

activity.prompt: Define `struct P { char name[20]; int marks; };`. Read n then n lines of `name marks`; print the name with the highest marks (first one on ties).
activity.hint: Track the index of the best record; use > (not >=) to keep the first on ties.

quiz.q: Access member x through pointer p to a struct?
quiz.why: For a pointer to a struct, p->x means (*p).x, so it dereferences the pointer and selects the member.

quiz.q: Can two structs be compared with ==?
quiz.why: C doesn't define == for structures. You must compare the members one by one (or use memcmp with care).

quiz.q: A struct can contain a member of type…
quiz.why: A struct can't contain an instance of itself, since it would be infinitely large. It can contain a pointer to itself, which is how linked lists are built.

quiz.q: `s2 = s1;` for two structs of the same type…
quiz.why: Assigning one struct to another of the same type copies all of its members.

options: Create an alias for a type
quiz.why: typedef gives a new name (an alias) to an existing type. It doesn't create a new type or allocate memory.

scenes.text: Kunal expects his struct of a char and an int to take 5 bytes, but sizeof says 8.
The compiler inserted padding so the int sits on a 4-byte boundary, which the CPU reads faster.

steps.title: Alignment and padding
steps.body:
Typical rule (4-byte int, 8-byte double): each member starts at an offset that is a multiple of its alignment, and the total size is a multiple of the largest member alignment.

- `struct A { char c; int i; };` → c at 0, padding 1–3, i at 4 → **8**.
- `struct B { char c; double d; char e; };` → c 0, d 8, e 16, total rounded to 24.
- Reordering largest-first: `{ double d; char c; char e; }` → 16.

Padding is implementation-defined; these values are for common 64-bit systems.

steps.title: Unions and enums
steps.body:
- **union**: all members share the same memory; size = largest member (plus padding). Only one member is meaningful at a time.
- `union U { int i; char c[4]; float f; };` → sizeof 4.
- **enum**: named integer constants. `enum Day { MON, TUE, WED = 10, THU };` → MON = 0, TUE = 1, WED = 10, THU = 11.
- **Bit-fields**: `struct F { unsigned ready : 1; unsigned mode : 3; };` packs flags into bits; you cannot take the address of a bit-field.

steps.title: Solved example: sizeof questions
steps.body:
Assume char 1, short 2, int 4, double 8 bytes with natural alignment.
- `struct { char a; short b; char c; }` → a 0, b 2, c 4, size rounded to multiple of 2 → **6**.
- `struct { int x; char y; }` → 5 rounded up to **8**.
- `union { double d; int a[3]; }` → largest member 12, rounded to multiple of 8 → **16**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding member sizes and ignoring padding.
- Writing one union member and reading another, expecting a portable conversion (type punning has subtle rules).
- Assuming enum values must be consecutive or start at 1.

activity.prompt: Print the values of an enum `enum Level { LOW, MID = 5, HIGH, MAX = 20 };` as `LOW MID HIGH MAX` numbers on one line: expected `0 5 6 20`.
activity.hint: An enumerator without a value is one more than the previous one.

quiz.q: sizeof a union is at least…
quiz.why: All members of a union share the same memory, so a union is at least as big as its largest member.

quiz.q: `enum E { A, B = 4, C };` C equals…
quiz.why: Enumerators count up from the previous value. A = 0, B = 4, so C = 4 + 1 = 5.

quiz.q: Typical sizeof `struct { char c; int i; }` with 4-byte int?
quiz.why: The int must be aligned to 4 bytes, so 3 padding bytes are inserted after the char. The size is 1 + 3 + 4 = 8.

quiz.q: Can you take the address of a bit-field member?
quiz.why: Bit-fields may not start on a byte boundary, so they have no address and you can't use & on them.

quiz.q: Reordering struct members from largest to smallest usually…
quiz.why: Ordering members from largest to smallest usually needs less padding between them, so the struct gets smaller.

lessons.title: The preprocessor, macros and bit manipulation

scenes.text: Om defines #define SQ(x) x*x and SQ(2+3) gives 11 instead of 25.
Text substitution produced 2+3*2+3. Parentheses around every parameter and the whole body fix it.

steps.title: Directives
steps.body:
- `#include <file>` (system path) vs `#include "file"` (local first).
- `#define PI 3.14159` — object-like macro; `#define MAX(a,b) ((a) > (b) ? (a) : (b))` — function-like.
- `#undef`, `#if`, `#ifdef`, `#ifndef`, `#elif`, `#else`, `#endif` — conditional compilation.
- **Include guards**: `#ifndef MYLIB_H` / `#define MYLIB_H` … `#endif` prevent double inclusion.
- Operators: `#x` makes a string, `a##b` pastes tokens. Predefined: `__FILE__`, `__LINE__`, `__DATE__`.

steps.title: Solved example: macro traps
steps.body:
`#define SQ(x) x*x`
- SQ(2+3) → 2+3*2+3 = **11**.
- `#define SQ(x) ((x)*(x))` → 25. ✓
- But SQ(i++) → ((i++)*(i++)) modifies i twice → undefined. Prefer an `inline` function for such cases.

`#define DOUBLE(x) (x)+(x)` then `10 * DOUBLE(3)` → 10*(3)+(3) = **33**, not 60. Wrap the whole body in parentheses.

steps.title: Bit manipulation toolkit
steps.body:
- Set bit k: `x | (1u << k)`
- Clear bit k: `x & ~(1u << k)`
- Toggle bit k: `x ^ (1u << k)`
- Test bit k: `(x >> k) & 1`
- Is power of two: `x && !(x & (x - 1))`
- Count set bits (Kernighan): `while (x) { x &= x - 1; c++; }` — runs once per set bit.
- Swap without temp: `a ^= b; b ^= a; a ^= b;` (fails if a and b are the same object).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Missing parentheses in macros.
- A space between macro name and '(' in the definition makes it object-like: `#define F (x) x` is not a function-like macro.
- Shifting a signed negative number or shifting by ≥ the width of the type — undefined.

activity.prompt: Read an unsigned integer x. Print the number of set bits, and `yes` or `no` for whether x is a power of two, on two lines.
activity.hint: x & (x-1) clears the lowest set bit; keep a copy of x for the second test.

quiz.why: The macro just replaces text: SQ(1+1) becomes 1+1*1+1. Multiplication goes first, so it is 1 + 1 + 1 = 3, not 4. Wrap macro parameters in parentheses.

options: Prevent multiple inclusion of a header
quiz.why: Include guards (#ifndef / #define / #endif) stop a header from being included twice in the same file, which avoids redefinition errors.

quiz.q: Expression to test whether bit 3 of x is set?
quiz.why: Shift bit 3 down to position 0 with x >> 3, and mask with & 1 to get just that bit. Non-zero means it is set.
x − 1 flips the lowest set bit and all zeros below it. ANDing with x clears just the lowest set bit. This is Kernighan's trick.
Macros are expanded by the preprocessor, before the compiler sees the code.

scenes.text: Ananya's marks program loses all data when it closes, so she must re-type it every time.
She learns to write records to a file with fprintf and read them back with fscanf next time.

steps.title: The FILE workflow
steps.body:
- `FILE *fp = fopen("marks.txt", "r");` — returns NULL if it fails (always check).
- Modes: `"r"` read (must exist), `"w"` write (creates/truncates), `"a"` append, `"r+"` read/write (must exist), `"w+"` read/write (truncates), `"a+"` read/append; add `b` for binary (`"rb"`).
- Text I/O: `fprintf`, `fscanf`, `fgets`, `fputs`, `fgetc`, `fputc`.
- Binary I/O: `fwrite(&rec, sizeof rec, 1, fp)`, `fread(...)`.
- Positioning: `fseek(fp, offset, SEEK_SET|SEEK_CUR|SEEK_END)`, `ftell`, `rewind`.
- `fclose(fp)` flushes buffers and releases the file.

steps.title: Solved example: count lines in a file
Command-line arguments
steps.body:
`int main(int argc, char *argv[])`
- argc = number of arguments including the program name.
- argv[0] = program name, argv[1]… = arguments, argv[argc] = NULL.
- `./sum 3 4` → argc = 3, argv[1] = "3". Convert with `atoi` or `strtol`.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Not checking fopen for NULL.
- Opening with "w" when you meant to keep existing data (it truncates).
- `while (!feof(fp))` loops — they run one extra time; test the return value of the read function instead.
- Storing fgetc's result in a char.

activity.prompt: Simulate reading a file from standard input: count characters, words (separated by spaces/newlines) and lines until EOF, and print them as `chars words lines`. Use getchar like fgetc.
activity.hint: A word starts when you see a non-space character while 'in' is 0.

quiz.q: Mode that creates a file or erases an existing one?
quiz.why: Mode "w" opens a file for writing, creating it if it doesn't exist and truncating (erasing) it if it does. "a" appends instead.
fopen returns NULL if it can't open the file, so you should always check for it before using the file pointer.

quiz.q: Why store fgetc's result in an int?
options: To tell EOF apart from valid characters
quiz.why: EOF is a negative int value that doesn't correspond to a valid character. Storing the result in a char could confuse EOF with a real character, so use an int.
argv[0] is the program name, then 'a' and 'b'. That is 3 arguments, so argc is 3.

quiz.q: Function to move to the end of a file?
quiz.why: fseek(fp, 0, SEEK_END) moves the file position to the end. rewind goes to the start and ftell only reports the position.

questions.q: Operator to access a member through a struct pointer?
questions.why: For a pointer p to a struct, the -> operator accesses a member: p->m. The dot operator is for a struct variable.

questions.q: File mode "a" means…
questions.why: Mode "a" opens a file for appending: new data is written at the end and existing content stays.

questions.q: Typical sizeof `union { int i; double d; char c; }` on 64-bit?
questions.why: A union's size is that of its largest member. The double is 8 bytes, so the size is 8.

questions.q: `enum { R = 2, G, B = 7, Y };` values of G and Y?
questions.why: R = 2, so G = 3, and B = 7 is set explicitly, so Y = 8.

questions.q: With `#define ADD(a,b) a+b`, value of `3 * ADD(2,4)`?
questions.why: The macro substitutes text without parentheses, so 3 * ADD(2,4) becomes 3 * 2 + 4. By precedence this is 6 + 4 = 10, not 3 × 6 = 18.

questions.q: Typical sizeof `struct { char a; double b; int c; }` (8-byte double, 4-byte int)?
questions.why: char a at offset 0; the double b needs 8-byte alignment so it starts at 8; int c at 16. The total of 20 is padded to a multiple of 8, giving 24.

questions.q: Typical sizeof `struct { double b; int c; char a; }`?
questions.why: double b at 0, int c at 8, char a at 12. That's 13 bytes, padded to a multiple of 8 for the double, so 16.

questions.q: Expression to clear bit 2 of x?
questions.why: To clear bit 2, AND with the inverted mask: x & ~4. OR sets a bit, XOR toggles it, and x & 4 only tests it.

questions.q: Number of loop iterations of Kernighan's bit count for x = 0b10110010?
questions.why: Each iteration x &= x − 1 removes one set bit. The pattern 10110010 has four 1 bits, so the loop runs 4 times.

questions.q: Assertion: a struct may contain a member of its own type. Reason: the compiler can compute its size recursively.
questions.why: It may only contain a pointer to its own type; a self-instance would have infinite size.

questions.q: Case: A program reads a file with `while(!feof(fp)) { fscanf(fp, "%d", &x); sum += x; }` and the last number is added twice. Fix?
questions.why: feof only becomes true after a read has already failed, so the loop body runs once more with a stale x. Loop on the return value instead: while (fscanf(...) == 1).

questions.q: `x && !(x & (x-1))` is true for x =…
questions.why: x & (x − 1) is 0 only for powers of two (one set bit), and x && makes sure x isn't 0. Of the options, only 16 is a power of two.

questions.q: What does `#x` do inside a macro body?
options: Converts argument x to a string literal
questions.why: In a macro, #x is the stringizing operator. It turns the macro argument into a string literal, as in #define STR(x) #x.

questions.q: For `./calc 10 20 +`, argv[3] is…
questions.why: argv[0] is the program name "./calc", argv[1] is "10", argv[2] is "20", and argv[3] is "+".

questions.q: Which is FALSE about structures in C?
options: They can be passed by value
They can be returned from functions
questions.why: Structs can be passed by value, assigned and returned from functions, but == isn't defined for them. That's the false statement.

questions.q: Output: `unsigned x = 5; x ^= (1u << 1); printf("%u", x);`
questions.why: 1u << 1 is 2 (binary 0010). XOR with x = 5 (0101) gives 0111 = 7. The bit flips on.

questions.q: `#define MUL(a,b) ((a)*(b))` — value of MUL(1+2, 3+4)?
questions.why: The parameters are parenthesised, so MUL(1+2, 3+4) expands to ((1+2)*(3+4)) = 3 × 7 = 21. Without the parentheses it would become 1+2*3+4 = 11.

questions.q: Typical sizeof `struct { char a; short b; int c; char d; }` (short 2, int 4)?
questions.why: a at 0, short b at 2, int c at 4, char d at 8. That's 9 bytes, padded to a multiple of 4 (the largest alignment), so 12.

courses.title: Programming in C · Revision & Practice
courses.summary: One-page cheat sheets for every unit, a set of output-prediction drills, and two mock papers mixing all units at GATE and end-semester level.
outcomes: Learners can recall key rules of every unit quickly
Learners can predict outputs of tricky C snippets
Learners can attempt a full mock paper under time pressure

scenes.text: It is 10 pm before the C exam. Pooja has no time to reread notes.
She revises one compact sheet per unit and solves five tricky snippets.

steps.title: Unit 1 essentials
steps.body:
- Build: preprocess → compile → assemble → link.
- sizeof(char) = 1; int usually 4; signed overflow = UB; unsigned wraps mod 2ⁿ.
- Octal 0…, hex 0x…; 'A' = 65.
- Integer division truncates toward zero; sign of % follows dividend.
- && and || short-circuit; assignment and ?: are right-associative.
- %d %u %ld %lld %f (printf double) %lf (scanf double) %c %s %p %zu.

steps.title: Unit 2 essentials
steps.body:
- else pairs with nearest unmatched if.
- switch: integer type, constant labels, fall-through without break.
- do-while runs ≥ 1 time; for(;;) is infinite.
- Iteration counts: i *= k loops → log_k n; nested i, j ≤ i → n(n+1)/2.
- break exits innermost loop; continue jumps to the update (for).

steps.title: Unit 3 essentials
steps.body:
- Call by value; use pointers to modify caller variables.
- Storage: auto (garbage), static (0, persists), extern (declared elsewhere), register (no &).
- Recursion = base case + progress; frames on the stack.
- Hanoi 2ⁿ − 1; naive fib calls C(n) = 1 + C(n−1) + C(n−2).

steps.title: Drill with answers
steps.body:
- `printf("%d", 5 > 3 > 1);` → (1) > 1 → **0**.
- `int i = 3; printf("%d", i << 2 | 1);` → 12 | 1 = **13**.
- `int x = 7; x = x++ ;` — undefined behaviour in C before C11 sequencing rules too; avoid.
- `for (i = 0; i < 10; i += 3);` final i = **12**.

statements.s: sizeof(int) is always 4 bytes.
do-while executes its body at least once.
statements.why: The test is at the end.

statements.s: A static local variable is re-initialised on every call.
In C, -7 / 2 equals -3.
A switch can test a float value.

quiz.why: Comparison operators go left to right. 5 > 3 is 1, and then 1 > 1 is 0, so the result is 0, not true as maths would suggest.

quiz.q: Default value of an uninitialised auto variable?
quiz.why: An uninitialised auto variable holds an indeterminate (garbage) value. Only static and global variables are zero-initialised.
i goes 0, 3, 6, 9, then 12. Since 12 < 10 is false, the loop stops with i = 12.
'Undefined reference' is reported by the linker, when a symbol can't be resolved. Syntax and type errors come from the compiler.
Tower of Hanoi needs 2ⁿ − 1 moves: 2⁶ − 1 = 64 − 1 = 63.

scenes.text: Pointers still scare Imran. He decides to master just six identities.
With those six rules, every pointer question in the mock suddenly looks familiar.

steps.title: Unit 4 essentials
steps.body:
- addr(a[i]) = B + i·w; row-major A[i][j] = B + (i·C + j)·w; column-major = B + (j·R + i)·w.
- Arrays decay to pointers when passed; pass n separately.
- Bubble sort: n(n−1)/2 comparisons worst, O(n) best with flag, stable.
- Strings end with '\0'; strcmp for comparison; sizeof vs strlen.

steps.title: Unit 5 essentials
steps.body:
- a[i] ≡ *(a+i) ≡ i[a]; p + k moves k elements.
- *p++ (use, then move), (*p)++ (increment value), ++*p, *++p.
- &a + 1 skips the whole array.
- int *a[5] (array of pointers) vs int (*a)[5] (pointer to array).
- malloc (garbage) / calloc (zeros) / realloc (use temp) / free (then NULL).

steps.title: Unit 6 essentials
steps.body:
- Struct size includes padding; total is a multiple of the largest alignment.
- Union size = largest member (rounded).
- enum values continue from previous + 1.
- Macros: parenthesise parameters and body.
- Bits: set |, clear & ~, toggle ^, test >> & 1; x & (x−1) clears lowest set bit.
- fopen modes r/w/a/+/b; check NULL; loop on read return values.

steps.title: Drill with answers
steps.body:
- `char s[] = "GATE"; printf("%c", *(s + 3));` → **E**.
- `int a[] = {2,4,6}; int *p = a; p++; printf("%d", *p * 2);` → **8**.
- sizeof `struct { int a; char b; }` → **8** (typical).

activity.prompt: Match each declaration to its meaning.
pairs: pointer to an array of 4 ints

quiz.why: s + 1 points to the second character of 'CODE', so printf with %s prints from there to the end: 'ODE'.

quiz.q: Row-major address of A[1][2] in int A[3][3], base 100, w 4?
calloc differs from malloc because it…
quiz.why: calloc sets the allocated memory to zero. malloc leaves it holding garbage.
CUBE(1+1) expands to 1+1*1+1*1+1. Multiplications go first, so it is 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 4, not 8.

quiz.q: Typical sizeof `struct { char c[3]; int i; }`?
quiz.why: The 3 chars take 3 bytes, then 1 byte of padding so the int starts at offset 4. With the 4-byte int the total is 8.

lessons.title: Mock paper strategy and practice set

scenes.text: Yash used to get stuck on one hard pointer question and run out of time.
Now he does a first pass of easy questions, marks the hard ones, and returns to them later. His score rises by 15 marks.

steps.title: Exam strategy
steps.body:
- Pass 1: definitions, syntax, single-step outputs (aim for 40% of marks fast).
- Pass 2: tracing loops and recursion — write variable tables.
- Pass 3: pointer and memory puzzles — draw boxes and arrows.
- In programs: write the function signature, base cases and edge cases (n = 0, negative numbers, empty strings).

steps.title: Answer-writing for theory questions
steps.body:
- Define the term in one line.
- Give syntax.
- Give a short code example with output.
- Mention one advantage and one pitfall.

Example: 'Explain static storage class' → definition, syntax, counter example, 'persists across calls / not thread-safe as shared state'.

steps.title: Worked long question
steps.body:
Q: Write a function to remove duplicates from a sorted array in place and return the new length.
- Step 1: if n == 0 return 0.
- Step 2: k = 1; for i = 1 to n−1: if a[i] != a[k−1] then a[k++] = a[i].
- Step 3: return k.
- {1,1,2,3,3,3,4} → {1,2,3,4}, length **4**. Time O(n), space O(1).

steps.title: Last-minute traps
steps.body:
- Integer division inside averages.
- Missing break in switch.
- String compare with ==.
- Missing '\0' space.
- Off-by-one loop bounds.

activity.prompt: Remove duplicates from a sorted array in place. Read n and n sorted integers; print the new length, then the unique elements.
activity.hint: Keep a write index k; copy a[i] only when it differs from the last kept value.

quiz.q: Best first step when a recursion question looks hard?
quiz.why: Drawing the recursion tree lets you see each call and its result, which avoids tracing mistakes. Guessing isn't reliable.

quiz.q: Time complexity of in-place dedup of a sorted array?
quiz.why: A sorted array's duplicates sit next to each other, so one pass with two indices removes them in place in O(n).

quiz.q: Which edge case is most often forgotten in array functions?
quiz.why: The empty case (n = 0) is the one most often forgotten. Array functions may then read a[0] or a[n−1], which is out of range.

quiz.q: Average of ints a and b without truncation?
quiz.why: (a+b)/2 is integer division and drops the fraction. Dividing by 2.0 makes it floating-point, so the half is kept.
strcmp(s, t) == 0 compares the characters of the two strings. s == t only compares addresses.

questions.q: Mock 1 · Q1. Which header declares printf?
questions.why: printf is declared in <stdio.h>, the standard input/output header.

questions.q: Mock 1 · Q2. Output: `int a = 10; printf("%d", a++ + 5);`
questions.why: a++ gives the old value 10 in the expression, then increments a. So 10 + 5 = 15 is printed.

questions.q: Mock 1 · Q3. Iterations: `for(i=2;i<=50;i*=2)`
questions.why: i takes 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, and 64 fails i <= 50. That's 5 iterations.

questions.q: Mock 1 · Q4. `char *p = "hello"; printf("%c", p[strlen(p)-1]);`
questions.why: strlen(p) is 5, so p[4] is the last character of 'hello', 'o'. p[5] would be '\0'.

questions.q: Mock 1 · Q5. Return of `int f(int n){ return n<=0 ? 0 : n%2 + f(n/2); }` for n = 29?
questions.why: The function adds n%2 at each halving, which sums the binary digits of n. 29 is 11101, which has four 1 bits, so it returns 4.

questions.q: Mock 1 · Q6. Typical sizeof `struct { char a; int b; char c; }`?
questions.why: a at 0, int b needs alignment so it is at 4, c at 8. That's 9 bytes, padded to a multiple of 4, giving 12.

questions.q: Mock 1 · Q7. `int a[] = {1,2,3,4,5}; int *p = a + 4; printf("%d", p - a);`
questions.why: Pointer subtraction counts elements, not bytes: p − a with p = a + 4 gives 4.

questions.q: Mock 1 · Q8. Which causes a memory leak?
options: Reassigning the only pointer to a malloc'd block
questions.why: A leak happens when the last pointer to a malloc'd block is overwritten, because the block becomes unreachable and can't be freed. free(NULL) is harmless.

questions.q: Mock 2 · Q1. Value of 0x10 + 010 + 10?
questions.why: 0x10 is 16, 010 is octal = 8, and 10 is 10. The sum is 16 + 8 + 10 = 34.

questions.q: Mock 2 · Q2. `switch(1){ case 1: x+=1; case 2: x+=2; default: x+=3; }` with x = 0 gives x =
questions.why: The value 1 matches case 1: x = 1. With no break it falls through to case 2 (x = 3) and then default (x = 6).

questions.q: Mock 2 · Q3. Recursive calls (including the first) for `f(n){ if(n>1){ f(n-1); f(n-1);} }` with n = 4?
questions.why: C(n) = 1 + 2C(n−1) with C(1) = 1. That gives 1, 3, 7, 15 for n = 1 to 4, so f(4) makes 15 calls.

questions.q: Mock 2 · Q4. `int x = 0; if (x++ || ++x) ; printf("%d", x);`
questions.why: x++ gives 0 (false) and x becomes 1. Since the left side of || is false, ++x runs, making x = 2.

questions.q: Mock 2 · Q5. Column-major address of A[2][3] in A[4][5], base 0, w = 2?
questions.why: Column-major address = (col × rows + row) × size = (3 × 4 + 2) × 2 = 14 × 2 = 28.

questions.q: Mock 2 · Q6. `const int *p` and `int *const q` — which can be re-pointed?
questions.why: const int *p points to a const int, but p itself can be moved. int *const q is a constant pointer that can't be re-pointed. So only p can be re-pointed.

questions.q: Mock 2 · Q7. Case: A queue program crashes only after many runs; Valgrind reports 'invalid read of size 4' after free. Bug type?
questions.why: Valgrind reporting an invalid read after free means the program is using memory it already freed. That's a use-after-free bug.

questions.q: Mock 2 · Q8. Output: `int a=3, b=4; int *p=&a, *q=&b; *p ^= *q; *q ^= *p; *p ^= *q; printf("%d %d", a, b);`
questions.why: This is the XOR swap: a ^= b, b ^= a, a ^= b exchanges the two values without a temporary. So a = 4 and b = 3.

questions.q: Mock 2 · Q9. With `int a = -1; unsigned b = 1;`, `a > b` is…
questions.why: a is converted to unsigned, so −1 becomes a huge value (UINT_MAX), which is greater than 1. The result is 1.

questions.q: Mock 2 · Q10. Which is NOT valid C?
questions.why: An array name isn't a modifiable lvalue, so you can't assign to it. int a[3]; a = NULL; is invalid, while the other declarations are fine.

uni-cse-cloud.title: Cloud Computing
uni-cse-cloud.description: Cloud concepts, virtualisation and containers, core compute/storage/network services, serverless and DevOps, and security, identity, cost and reliability — vendor-neutral with AWS, Azure and Google Cloud examples.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Cloud Concepts and Models
courses.summary: The NIST definition of cloud computing, service models (IaaS, PaaS, SaaS), deployment models, economics (CapEx vs OpEx) and global infrastructure. Independent practice material; not affiliated with or endorsed by the exam provider. Check the official exam guide for the current skills outline.
outcomes: Learners can state the five essential characteristics of cloud computing
Learners can classify services as IaaS, PaaS, SaaS or FaaS
Learners can compare public, private, hybrid and multi-cloud deployments
Learners can explain regions, availability zones and edge locations

scenes.text: Every year a university's results website crashes when lakhs of students log in at 10 am.
Moving to the cloud, it scales out to 50 servers for two hours and back to 2 — paying only for what it used.

steps.title: NIST's five essential characteristics
steps.body:
The US National Institute of Standards and Technology (SP 800-145) defines cloud by:

- **On-demand self-service** — provision without calling a person.
- **Broad network access** — over standard networks from many devices.
- **Resource pooling** — multi-tenant shared hardware.
- **Rapid elasticity** — scale out/in quickly, appearing unlimited.
- **Measured service** — usage is metered and billed.

steps.title: Why organisations adopt cloud
steps.body:
- **CapEx → OpEx**: no up-front data-centre purchase; pay-as-you-go.
- Elasticity and global reach in minutes.
- Economies of scale lower unit cost.
- Managed services reduce operational work.
- Trade-offs: vendor lock-in, data-residency rules, variable bills, need for new skills.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1. Elasticity vs scalability.** Scalability = ability to handle growth (add resources). Elasticity = **automatically** adding and removing resources as demand changes. The results website shows elasticity.

**Example 2. Cost comparison.** On-premises: buy 50 servers for peak = ₹1.5 crore + running costs, idle 360 days a year. Cloud: 2 servers always + 48 extra for ~40 hours a year → a small fraction of the cost.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking cloud is always cheaper — steady, predictable workloads can be cheaper on reserved capacity or on-premises.
- 'Cloud = someone else's computer' ignores managed services and automation.
- Forgetting to switch off resources (idle resources still cost money).

activity.prompt: Match each NIST characteristic to its example.
pairs: Create a VM from a web console in 2 minutes
Use the app from a phone or laptop
Many customers share the same physical hosts
Billed per second of compute used

quiz.q: Which is NOT a NIST essential characteristic?
quiz.why: NIST's five essential characteristics are on-demand self-service, broad network access, resource pooling, rapid elasticity and measured service. 'Unlimited free storage' isn't one of them.

quiz.q: Moving from buying servers to monthly bills is a shift from…
quiz.why: Buying servers is a capital expense (CapEx). Paying a monthly bill for use is an operating expense (OpEx), so the shift is CapEx to OpEx.

quiz.q: Automatically adding and removing capacity with demand is…
quiz.why: Elasticity means capacity grows and shrinks automatically with demand, so you pay only for what you need.

quiz.q: A drawback of public cloud can be…
quiz.why: Public cloud services can be proprietary, which makes moving away hard. That's vendor lock-in.
Many customers (tenants) sharing the same physical infrastructure is resource pooling, one of NIST's characteristics.

lessons.title: Service models: IaaS, PaaS, SaaS, FaaS

scenes.text: Make pizza at home (on-premises), buy a frozen one and bake it (IaaS), order delivery (PaaS), or eat at a restaurant (SaaS).
The more 'as a service', the less you manage yourself.

steps.title: Who manages what
steps.body:
- **IaaS**: provider runs hardware, network, virtualisation; you manage OS, runtime, apps, data. (Virtual machines: EC2, Azure VMs, Compute Engine.)
- **PaaS**: provider also runs OS and runtime; you deploy code and data. (App Service, Elastic Beanstalk, App Engine, managed databases.)
- **SaaS**: complete application; you manage users and data settings. (Email, office suites, CRM.)
- **FaaS / serverless**: you upload functions that run on events and bill per invocation (Lambda, Azure Functions, Cloud Functions).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1. Classify.** A VM where you install Linux and MySQL → IaaS. A managed PostgreSQL service → PaaS (DBaaS). Web email → SaaS. A function that resizes images when uploaded → FaaS.

**Example 2. Patching.** Who patches the OS? IaaS → **you**. PaaS → **provider**. SaaS → **provider**.

steps.title: Choosing a model
steps.body: Prefer the highest-level service that meets your needs (less operations work); drop to IaaS when you need OS-level control, special software or lift-and-shift migration.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking SaaS means the provider is responsible for your data's correctness and access settings — you still own users, permissions and data.
- Calling any website 'SaaS'.
- Assuming serverless means no servers exist (they are just managed for you).

activity.prompt: Classify each offering.

items.text: Virtual machine with your own OS config
Managed web-app hosting where you push code
Virtual network and disks you configure

quiz.why: In IaaS the provider runs the hardware, networking and hypervisor. The customer manages the guest OS, middleware and applications.

quiz.q: A managed database service is typically…
quiz.why: A managed database service gives you a ready-made platform, with the provider handling the servers and database software. That's PaaS.

quiz.q: Serverless functions are billed mainly by…
quiz.why: Serverless functions are billed per invocation and for the time and memory they use, not for idle servers.

quiz.q: OS patching in PaaS is done by…
quiz.why: In PaaS the provider manages the platform, including OS patching. The customer manages just the application and data.
IaaS has the lowest level of abstraction, so the customer controls the most, down to the operating system.

scenes.text: A bank must keep core transaction data in its own controlled environment but wants cloud elasticity for its mobile app.
It chooses hybrid cloud: private for the core, public for the app front end, connected securely.

steps.title: The four (+1) models
steps.body:
- **Public cloud**: shared provider infrastructure, open to any customer.
- **Private cloud**: dedicated to one organisation, on-premises or hosted.
- **Hybrid cloud**: private + public connected, workloads can move between them.
- **Community cloud**: shared by organisations with common concerns (e.g. government departments).
- **Multi-cloud**: using several public providers (avoid lock-in, best-of-breed, resilience).

steps.title: Data residency and compliance
steps.body: Laws and regulators may require certain data to stay within a country or meet specific controls. In India, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023 governs personal data, and sector regulators (for example for banking and payments) may add rules. Providers offer in-country regions to help customers comply — but compliance remains the customer's responsibility too.

steps.title: Solved examples
