courses.title: Unit 7 · Application Layer & Network Security
courses.summary: DNS, HTTP (versions, methods, status codes, cookies, caching), email (SMTP, POP3, IMAP), FTP, SSH, and network security: symmetric and public-key cryptography (RSA, Diffie–Hellman), hashing, digital signatures, certificates, TLS, firewalls and VPNs.
outcomes: Learners can trace a DNS resolution and an HTTP request
Learners can compute HTTP response times for persistent and non-persistent connections
Learners can do a toy RSA and Diffie–Hellman exchange
Learners can explain how TLS provides confidentiality, integrity and authentication

scenes.text: Typing example.com needs an IP address first.
DNS asks a hierarchy: root → .com → example.com's authoritative server.

steps.title: How DNS works
steps.body:
Distributed hierarchical database: **root** servers → **TLD** servers (.com, .in) → **authoritative** servers; plus local/recursive resolvers with caches (TTL). Queries: **recursive** (resolver does all the work for the client) and **iterative** (server replies with a referral). Mostly UDP port 53; TCP 53 for large responses and zone transfers.
Records: **A** (IPv4), **AAAA** (IPv6), **CNAME** (alias), **MX** (mail server), **NS** (name server), **TXT**, **PTR** (reverse), **SOA**.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Counting queries
steps.body: Cold cache, iterative resolution of www.example.com by the local resolver: root → .com TLD → example.com authoritative → **3 queries** (plus the host's 1 recursive query to the resolver). If the .com TLD address is cached, only 2.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Which record?
steps.body:
- Mail for user@college.edu.in → look up **MX** of college.edu.in.
- blog.site.com is an alias of site.github.io → **CNAME**.
- IP → name for logs → **PTR**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying DNS uses only TCP.
- Confusing recursive (client side) and iterative (between servers).
- Forgetting caches and TTLs when counting queries.

activity.prompt: Match the DNS record

quiz.why: DNS queries are small, so they mostly use UDP port 53. TCP is used for large responses and zone transfers.

quiz.q: A referral reply is part of
quiz.why: In an iterative query, a server replies with a referral, 'ask this other server', and the resolver goes on to query it itself.

options: how long a record may be cached
quiz.why: DNS TTL says how long a resolver may cache a record before asking again.
Zone transfers copy a lot of data, so they use TCP for reliable delivery.

quiz.q: Highest level of the DNS hierarchy
quiz.why: The root servers sit at the top of the DNS hierarchy, followed by the TLD servers and then the authoritative servers.

scenes.text: A news homepage has 1 HTML file and 10 images.
Whether connections are reused decides if it loads in 3 RTTs or 22.

steps.title: HTTP essentials
steps.body:
Request: method (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, PATCH, HEAD, OPTIONS), URL, headers, body. Response: status code + headers + body. Status classes: 1xx info, **2xx success** (200 OK, 201 Created, 204), **3xx redirect** (301, 302, 304 Not Modified), **4xx client error** (400, 401, 403, 404), **5xx server error** (500, 502, 503).
HTTP is stateless; **cookies** add state. Conditional GET (If-Modified-Since / ETag) and caches/CDNs reduce load.
Versions: 1.0 non-persistent by default; **1.1 persistent** (keep-alive); **HTTP/2** binary framing, multiplexed streams over one TCP connection, header compression; **HTTP/3** over QUIC (UDP), avoiding TCP head-of-line blocking.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Response time
steps.body:
Base HTML + 10 small objects, transmission time ignored.
- Non-persistent, serial: each object needs 2 RTT (TCP setup + request/response) → 11 × 2 = **22 RTT**.
- Non-persistent with 5 parallel connections: 2 (base) + 2 × 2 (two rounds of 5) = **6 RTT**.
- Persistent with pipelining: 2 (base) + 1 (all 10 together) = **3 RTT**.
- Persistent without pipelining: 2 + 10 = **12 RTT**.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Status codes
steps.body: Browser re-requests a cached logo with If-Modified-Since; it has not changed → **304 Not Modified** (no body). Wrong password → **401**; logged in but not allowed → **403**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying HTTP/2 runs over UDP (HTTP/3 does).
- Confusing 401 (not authenticated) and 403 (forbidden).
- Forgetting the TCP handshake RTT for each new connection.

activity.prompt: Non-persistent HTTP, serial, base page + 6 referenced objects, ignore transmission time. Total time in RTTs?

quiz.why: HTTP/1.1 connections are persistent by default, so several requests can reuse one TCP connection.
HTTP 304 means 'not modified': the client's cached copy is still valid, so no body is sent.
HTTP/3 runs over QUIC, which itself uses UDP. HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 use TCP.
HTTP is stateless, so cookies let a server recognise the same client across requests and keep session state.

quiz.q: Which method should be idempotent and safe?
quiz.why: GET is a safe method: it only reads and doesn't change the server, and repeating it gives the same result. POST isn't idempotent.

lessons.title: Email, file transfer and remote login

scenes.text: Priya's mail client pushes her message to her mail server, which pushes it to the recipient's server.
The recipient's app pulls it with IMAP or POP3.

steps.title: Protocols and ports
steps.body:
- **SMTP** (TCP 25; 587 for submission): push mail client → server → server.
- **POP3** (110 / 995 TLS): download, usually delete from server.
- **IMAP** (143 / 993 TLS): keep mail on server, folders, sync across devices.
- **MIME** extends email for attachments, non-ASCII text.
- **FTP**: control on TCP 21, data on 20 (active) or a negotiated port (passive) — 'out-of-band' control. **SFTP/FTPS** add security.
- **SSH** (22) replaces insecure **Telnet** (23).
- **DHCP** 67/68 (UDP), **SNMP** 161/162 (UDP), **HTTPS** 443.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Path of an email
steps.body: Alice (Gmail web) → HTTPS to Gmail → Gmail's SMTP server → recipient's SMTP server (MX lookup) → Bob's mailbox → Bob's phone pulls via IMAP. SMTP is used only for the **server-to-server push** and client submission.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Why FTP is 'out-of-band'
steps.body: Commands (USER, PASS, RETR) travel on port 21 while file bytes use a separate data connection, so a long download does not block new commands.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying POP3 or IMAP sends mail (they retrieve).
- Mixing up 21 (control) and 20 (data).
- Using Telnet across the Internet (plaintext passwords).

activity.prompt: Push or pull?

quiz.why: IMAP uses port 143 by default. POP3 uses 110, SMTP 25 and FTP 21.
SMTP is a push protocol: the sender's mail server pushes the message to the receiver's server. POP3 and IMAP are used to pull mail.
FTP's control connection uses port 21. Port 20 is classically used for the data connection.
SSH is the secure, encrypted replacement for Telnet, which sends everything, including passwords, in clear text.
MIME extends email to carry attachments and non-ASCII text, such as images and other languages.

scenes.text: Two friends share a secret key and lock messages with it — fast but how did they share the key?
Public-key crypto gives everyone an open padlock; only the owner has the key.

steps.title: Goals and tools
steps.body:
Confidentiality, integrity, authentication, non-repudiation, availability.
- **Symmetric** (same key): AES (block cipher, 128-bit blocks), ChaCha20; fast. n users need n(n − 1)/2 keys.
- **Public key**: RSA, elliptic-curve; slow, used for key exchange and signatures. n users need 2n keys (n pairs).
- **Hash functions** (SHA-256): fixed-size digest, one-way, collision resistant. **MAC/HMAC** = keyed hash for integrity + authenticity.
- **Digital signature:** sign hash with private key, verify with public key. **Certificates** (X.509) bind a public key to a name, signed by a CA.
- **TLS 1.3:** handshake with (EC)DHE key exchange + certificate authentication, then symmetric AEAD encryption.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Toy Diffie–Hellman
steps.body:
Public p = 23, g = 5. Alice secret a = 4 → A = 5⁴ mod 23 = 625 mod 23 = **4**. Bob secret b = 3 → B = 5³ mod 23 = 125 mod 23 = **10**.
Shared: Alice B^a = 10⁴ mod 23 = 18; Bob A^b = 4³ = 64 mod 23 = **18** ✓. An eavesdropper sees 4 and 10 but not 18 (discrete-log problem). Plain DH is vulnerable to man-in-the-middle without authentication.

steps.title: Network defences
steps.body: **Firewalls:** packet filters (stateless rules on IP/port), stateful firewalls (track connections), application gateways/proxies, next-gen (deep inspection). **IDS/IPS** detect/prevent attacks. **VPNs** (IPsec, TLS-based, WireGuard) tunnel traffic encrypted. Common attacks: DoS/DDoS, spoofing, man-in-the-middle, phishing, DNS poisoning (DNSSEC adds signatures).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Encrypting with the private key to keep a message secret (that is signing; for secrecy encrypt with the recipient's public key).
- Calling hashing encryption (it is one-way, no key to reverse).
- Thinking HTTPS hides the destination IP (it does not).

activity.prompt: Toy RSA with n = 33, e = 3. Encrypt the message m = 5 (c = m^e mod n).

quiz.q: To send a secret to Bob, encrypt with
quiz.why: To send a secret to Bob, encrypt it with Bob's public key. Only Bob's private key can decrypt it.
With pairwise symmetric keys, n users need n(n−1)/2 keys: 10 × 9/2 = 45.
A digital signature is made with the signer's private key, so anyone can verify it. It proves who signed (authentication) and prevents denial (non-repudiation).
TLS 1.3 uses public-key methods only for the handshake. The bulk data is encrypted with fast symmetric AEAD ciphers, such as AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305.
Plain Diffie–Hellman doesn't authenticate the parties, so a man-in-the-middle can set up separate keys with each side.

questions.q: DNS maps
questions.why: DNS translates names, like www.example.com, into IP addresses. It works like a phone book.

questions.q: HTTPS port
questions.why: HTTPS uses TCP port 443. HTTP uses 80.

questions.q: Which retrieves email and keeps it on the server?
questions.why: IMAP leaves mail on the server and lets you manage it from several devices. POP3 usually downloads it and removes it from the server.

questions.q: 404 means
questions.why: HTTP 404 means 'not found': the client asked for something the server doesn't have. It is a client error.

questions.q: SHA-256 is a
questions.why: SHA-256 is a cryptographic hash function that makes a fixed-size digest of data. It's not a cipher or a key exchange.

questions.q: Public-key pairs for 50 users
questions.why: In public-key cryptography each user needs only one key pair (a public and a private key), so 50 users need 50 pairs (100 keys).

questions.q: Assertion (A): HTTP/2 can suffer TCP head-of-line blocking. Reason (R): All its streams share one TCP connection. Choose:
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: A is true: HTTP/2 can suffer TCP head-of-line blocking. R is true and explains it, because all its streams share one TCP connection, and a lost packet stalls them all. HTTP/3 over QUIC avoids this.

questions.q: Persistent HTTP with pipelining, base + 20 objects: RTTs
questions.why: With a persistent connection and pipelining: 1 RTT for the TCP setup, 1 RTT for the base page, and 1 RTT to fetch all 20 objects together. That's 3 RTTs.
n = 55, φ = (5−1)(11−1) = 40. We need d with 3d ≡ 1 mod 40. d = 27 works because 3 × 27 = 81 = 2 × 40 + 1.

questions.q: Case: a site's users get a browser warning that the certificate is not trusted. Most likely cause
options: certificate not signed by a trusted CA / expired / wrong name
questions.why: Browsers show this warning when the certificate chain can't be validated: it isn't signed by a trusted CA, has expired, or the name doesn't match the site.

questions.q: Diffie–Hellman p = 11, g = 2, a = 3, b = 4. Shared secret
questions.why: A = 2³ mod 11 = 8, B = 2⁴ mod 11 = 5. Shared: 5³ mod 11 = 125 mod 11 = 4, and 8⁴ mod 11 = 4096 mod 11 = 4.

questions.q: Non-persistent HTTP, 3 parallel connections, base + 9 objects: RTTs
questions.why: The base page takes 2 RTTs (TCP setup plus request). The 9 objects are fetched in 3 rounds of 3 parallel connections, each round costing 2 RTTs, so 6 RTTs. Total is 2 + 6 = 8.

questions.q: Encrypt-then-MAC primarily ensures
questions.why: Encrypt-then-MAC encrypts the data and then authenticates the ciphertext, which gives both confidentiality and integrity. It is the idea behind AEAD.

questions.q: Iterative DNS lookup, cold cache, for a.b.example.org where b.example.org is a separate zone: queries by the resolver
questions.why: The resolver asks the root server, then the .org server, then the example.org server, and finally the b.example.org server, which is a separate zone. That's 4 queries.

questions.q: Which statement about firewalls is TRUE?
questions.why: A stateful firewall tracks the state of connections and allows replies to permitted traffic. Stateless filters look at each packet alone, and firewalls don't encrypt.

questions.q: A web page needs DNS (1 RTT), TCP setup (1 RTT), TLS 1.3 handshake (1 RTT), then the HTML request (1 RTT). Minimum RTTs before HTML arrives
questions.why: Count the round trips in order: DNS lookup 1, TCP handshake 1, TLS 1.3 handshake 1, and the HTML request/response 1. That is 4 RTTs.

courses.title: Revision & Practice · Computer Networks
courses.summary: Formula sheet, port and protocol tables, a mixed numerical drill and two mock papers covering all CN units.
outcomes: Learners can recall every CN formula and port
Learners can solve mixed numericals quickly
Learners can avoid frequent exam traps

scenes.text: Kiran condenses the whole course into one sheet.
Formulas on the left, traps on the right.

steps.title: Delays and capacity
steps.body:
- Tt = L/R; Tp = d/s; pipeline (N links, P packets): (N + P − 1)Tt + ΣTp
- Nyquist 2B log₂ L; Shannon B log₂(1 + SNR); SNR = 10^(dB/10)
- Stop-and-wait η = 1/(1 + 2a), a = Tp/Tt; window η = W/(1 + 2a)
- GBN W ≤ 2^k − 1; SR W ≤ 2^(k−1)

steps.title: MAC and IP
steps.body:
- Pure ALOHA S = Ge^(−2G), max 0.184; slotted S = Ge^(−G), max 0.368
- CSMA/CD L_min = 2·Tp·R
- Hosts = 2^(32 − n) − 2; block size = 256 − mask octet
- Fragment offset = data bytes before / 8
- Hamming: 2^r ≥ m + r + 1; detect d_min − 1, correct ⌊(d_min − 1)/2⌋

steps.title: TCP
steps.body:
- Throughput ≤ window/RTT
- Wrap time = 2³²/R(bytes/s)
- Timeout = EstRTT + 4 DevRTT (α 1/8, β 1/4)
- Slow start doubles to ssthresh; then +1; timeout → cwnd 1, ssthresh = cwnd/2; 3 dup ACKs → cwnd = ssthresh = cwnd/2

steps.title: Ports
steps.body: FTP 20/21 · SSH 22 · Telnet 23 · SMTP 25 (587) · DNS 53 · DHCP 67/68 · HTTP 80 · POP3 110 · IMAP 143 · SNMP 161 · BGP 179 · HTTPS 443 · RIP 520 (UDP) · OSPF IP protocol 89

steps.title: Top traps
steps.body:
- bytes vs bits; Mbps = 10⁶
- 2Tp (round trip) in efficiency and L_min
- usable hosts −2
- offsets in 8-byte units
- SYN/FIN consume one sequence number
- longest-prefix match, not first match

quiz.q: SR with 4-bit sequence numbers: max window
quiz.why: Selective Repeat's window is half the sequence space. With 4-bit numbers there are 16, so the maximum window is 2³ = 8.
A /28 has 4 host bits, which gives 16 addresses. Without the network and broadcast addresses, 14 are usable.
DHCP uses UDP, with port 67 for the server and port 68 for the client.
After a timeout, TCP sets cwnd to 1 MSS and restarts slow start.

scenes.text: One problem from each unit, 3 minutes each.
Follow the steps, then try the activity.

steps.title: Drill 1 · Delay
steps.body: Packet 1250 B on 100 Mbps, 200 km fibre (2 × 10⁸ m/s): Tt = 10⁴/10⁸ = 0.1 ms, Tp = 1 ms → **1.1 ms**.

steps.title: Drill 4 · Routing
steps.body: X: neighbours A (2), B (6). A: {Y: 5}, B: {Y: 0}. D_X(Y) = min(7, 6) = **6 via B**.

steps.title: Drill 5 · TCP
steps.body: ssthresh 20, cwnd 1: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 20, 21 … At RTT 9 cwnd = 23; timeout → ssthresh 11, cwnd 1.

activity.prompt: Network address of 10.10.75.130/21: what is the third octet?

quiz.why: Total delay is the sum of the two parts, 0.1 ms and 1 ms, giving 1.1 ms. They are two separate components, so you add them.
Efficiency is the useful time divided by the total time: 25/50 = 50%.
Block 72–79.
The lowest-cost route to the destination, with cost 6, goes through B, so B is the next hop.
The private exponent d satisfies e·d ≡ 1 mod φ. Here 7 × 43 = 301 = 5 × 60 + 1, so d = 43.

scenes.text: The course exam combines Paper A (concepts) and Paper B (numericals).
Target 45 minutes; review every explanation.

steps.title: Method
steps.body:
- Draw a timeline for protocol questions (handshakes, windows).
- Write units at every step.
- For subnetting, convert only the 'interesting' octet to binary.

steps.title: Mark-losing habits
steps.body:
- Forgetting the round-trip factor 2
- Mixing GBN and SR window limits
- Choosing first-match instead of longest prefix

steps.title: Interview link
steps.body: 'What happens when you type a URL?' — DNS (UDP 53), TCP handshake, TLS, HTTP request, routing via BGP/OSPF, ARP on the LAN. You can now explain each hop.

activity.prompt: I can…
items: Compute all four delays
Do CRC and Hamming by hand
Find stop-and-wait/GBN/SR efficiency
Subnet any prefix
Run Dijkstra and DV updates
Trace TCP seq/ACK and cwnd
Explain DNS, HTTP and TLS

quiz.why: A timeline (sequence) diagram shows each message and its timing, which makes protocol traces easy to follow.
For subnetting, concentrate on the interesting octet, the one where the mask is partial. The other octets are either all 255 or 0.
The factor 1 + 2a includes the round trip: the frame time plus two propagation delays, in units of Tt.
When you type a URL, the browser first needs the server's IP address, so it does a DNS lookup unless the answer is cached.

quiz.q: Which layer does TLS sit on?
quiz.why: TLS sits between the transport layer and the application, usually running over TCP and securing application data such as HTTP.

questions.q: [Paper A] Routers operate at
questions.why: Routers forward packets using IP addresses, so they work at layer 3, the network layer.

questions.q: [Paper A] CSMA/CA is used in
questions.why: Wi-Fi (802.11) uses CSMA/CA, collision avoidance. Ethernet uses CSMA/CD.

questions.q: [Paper A] Port for SSH
questions.why: SSH uses port 22. Port 21 is FTP, 23 is Telnet and 25 is SMTP.

questions.q: [Paper A] Which detects all single-bit errors and bursts ≤ r?
questions.why: A CRC detects all single-bit errors and all bursts up to its length r. Parity detects only odd numbers of errors.

questions.q: [Paper A] Switches separate
questions.why: Each switch port is its own collision domain, but all ports are in the same broadcast domain unless VLANs are used.

questions.q: [Paper A] BGP is a ___ protocol
questions.why: BGP is a path-vector protocol, as it advertises full AS paths.

questions.q: [Paper A] Assertion (A): UDP suits live voice. Reason (R): Retransmitted late packets are useless for real-time playback. Choose:
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: A is true: UDP suits live voice. R is true and explains it: a retransmitted packet would arrive too late to play, so TCP's reliability doesn't help real-time audio.

questions.q: [Paper A] IPv6 replaces ARP with
questions.why: IPv6 uses Neighbor Discovery (ICMPv6) instead of ARP to find link-layer addresses.

questions.q: [Paper A] HTTP/3 transport
questions.why: HTTP/3 runs over QUIC, which uses UDP.

questions.q: [Paper A] In TLS 1.3, certificates provide
questions.why: In TLS 1.3 a certificate proves the server's identity, so the client can authenticate the server.

questions.q: [Paper B] Hosts in /23
questions.why: A /23 has 9 host bits, so 2⁹ = 512 addresses and 510 usable hosts.

questions.q: [Paper B] Stop-and-wait, Tt = 5 ms, Tp = 10 ms: efficiency
[Paper B] CRC remainder of 100100 with 1101
questions.why: Append 3 zeros to 100100 to get 100100000, then divide by 1101 using XOR. The remainder is 001.

questions.q: [Paper B] CSMA/CD: 10 Mbps, Tp = 25.6 µs: L_min
questions.why: L_min = 2 × Tp × R = 2 × 25.6 µs × 10⁷ bps = 512 bits (64 bytes), the classic Ethernet minimum frame.

questions.q: [Paper B] Fragment offsets for 3000 B data, MTU 1500, header 20
questions.why: Each fragment carries 1480 bytes of data (1500 − 20). 3000 B splits into 1480, 1480 and 40, so the offsets are 0, 1480/8 = 185 and 2960/8 = 370.

questions.q: [Paper B] 192.168.100.0/24 into /26 subnets: broadcast of the 3rd subnet
questions.why: A /26 gives blocks of 64: .0, .64, .128, .192. The 3rd subnet is .128–.191, so its broadcast address is 192.168.100.191.

questions.q: [Paper B] TCP: ssthresh 6, cwnd values RTT 1–6
questions.why: cwnd doubles 1, 2, 4 and is capped at ssthresh 6 on the next step. After that it grows by 1 per RTT, giving 7, 8. So: 1, 2, 4, 6, 7, 8.

questions.q: [Paper B] Window 128 KB (131,072 B), RTT 200 ms: max throughput
questions.why: Throughput ≤ window/RTT = 131,072 × 8 bits / 0.2 s = 1,048,576/0.2 ≈ 5.24 × 10⁶ bps ≈ 5.24 Mbps.

questions.q: [Paper B] Pure ALOHA, 56 kbps channel, 1000-bit frames, stations together send 14 frames/s: throughput S
[Paper B] Hamming bits needed for 32 data bits
questions.why: Hamming needs 2ʳ ≥ m + r + 1. With m = 32: r = 5 gives 32 < 38, but r = 6 gives 64 ≥ 39. So 6 check bits.
